name: Bukhara
info: Bukhara is a city on the Zeravshan River in south-central Uzbekistan, founded officially in 500 BCE on the Silk Road, a capital of the Samanids and of the later Khanate and Emirate of Bukhara, and a centre of Islamic learning.

facts.founded: Officially in 500 BCE in the area now called the Ark, though the Bukhara oasis had been inhabited long before; in the Shahnameh the city was founded by King Siavash.
facts.where: On the Zeravshan River in south-central Uzbekistan, about 230 km west of Samarkand.
facts.known: A Silk Road trade centre; a Samanid capital and intellectual centre of the Islamic world; the birthplace of Imam Bukhari; the Kalan Minaret; the Karakhanid and Uzbek mosques and madrasas; the Emirate of Bukhara; the siege by Genghis Khan in 1220
facts.today: Bukhara is the capital of Bukhara Region in Uzbekistan, and its historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

t: Bukhara grew from three small fortified settlements of the Sogdian oasis into a walled city by 500 BCE, and passed from Persian rule to Alexander, the Seleucid Empire, the Greco-Bactrians, the Kushan Empire and the Turkic Kaganate, and then to the Arabs, who took it after long resistance in the 8th century.
As a capital of the Samanids it became an intellectual centre of the Islamic world, the Karakhanids built the Kalan Minaret, and Genghis Khan took the city in 1220 after a siege of fifteen days.
The Uzbek Khanate and the later Emirate of Bukhara ruled it until the Red Army attacked in 1920, and in 1924 the city became part of the Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic.
dyk: Narshakhi's History of Bukhara, completed in 943 to 944, records a fair at the bazaar of Makh at which idols were bought and sold, a practice that continued even after the Islamic conquest.
ev: Three small fortified settlements have grown together and been enclosed by a wall, and Bukhara enters history as a satrapy of the Persian Empire
Qutaiba ibn Muslim builds a grand mosque inside the citadel, on the site of a former temple
Bukhara becomes the capital of the Samanid Empire
Genghis Khan besieges Bukhara for fifteen days, and most of the city burns
Shah Murad formalises the dynastic rule of the Manghit family and the khanate becomes the Emirate of Bukhara
Red Army troops under Mikhail Frunze attack the city, and the emir flees
The Bukharan People's Soviet Republic is integrated into the Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic

sections.origins:
Bukhara stands on the Zeravshan River in south-central Uzbekistan, at an elevation of 229 metres. Its climate is cool and arid, with a mean annual precipitation of 135 millimetres, so from ancient times the oasis depended on irrigation, on canals and on uncovered reservoirs called hauzes. The oasis had been inhabited long before the city existed. The archaeologist E. E. Kuzmina links the Zaman-Baba culture of the third millennium BCE to the spread of Indo-Aryans across Central Asia, and from 3000 BCE a Bronze Age culture, the Sapalli, thrived at sites such as Varakhsha, Vardan, Paykend and Ramitan.

Around 1500 BCE climatic drying, iron technology and the arrival of Indo-Aryan nomads triggered a population shift to the oasis. By 1000 BCE the Sapalli and the Indo-Aryan people had merged into one culture, and around 700 BCE this culture, called Sogdian, flourished in city-states along the Zeravshan Valley. Three small fortified settlements had been built by then, and by 500 BCE they had grown together and were enclosed by a wall. The city is officially said to have been founded in 500 BCE in the area now called the Ark.

The Shahnameh gives another account. In the epic the city was founded by King Siavash, who built the Ark and the surrounding city in a vassal kingdom granted to him by Afrasiab, the king of Samarkand.
sections.growth:
Bukhara entered history in 500 BCE as a vassal state of the Persian Empire. It was a cult centre for the worship of Anahita, and about once in a lunar cycle the inhabitants of the Zeravshan Fan exchanged their old idols of the goddess for new ones at a trade festival held in front of the Mokh Temple. The festival made Bukhara a centre of commerce. A gold 20-stater of the Greco-Bactrian king Eucratides I, the largest gold coin ever minted in antiquity at 169.2 grams, was found in the city.

Trade quickened on the Silk Road after the Han dynasty pushed back the northern tribes, and the silk trade encouraged the rapid growth of the city, which ended around 350 CE. After the fall of the Kushan Empire the city entered a steep decline, but the 5th century saw unprecedented growth in urban and rural settlements throughout the oasis, which was surrounded by a wall more than 400 km long.

The city reached its greatest intellectual standing under the Samanids, when it was renowned for its numerous libraries and became a rival to Baghdad. Rudaki, called the father of Persian poetry, was born and raised there. The Samanid slave trade was the main income of the state. In 1070 the Song emperor Shenzong invited 5,300 Muslim men from Bukhara to China as mercenaries, and in 1080 a further 10,000 Muslims came.
sections.rulers:
Bukhara was a satrapy of the Persian Empire from 500 BCE, and then passed to Alexander the Great, the Seleucid Empire, the Greco-Bactrians and the Kushan Empire. After the Kushan Empire it fell to Hua tribes from the steppe. Between 563 and 567 the Turks of the Turkic Kaganate defeated the Hephtalites in a battle near the city, and Bukhara became dependent on the Kaganate. Arab armies arrived in 650 and found it ruled by the Bukhar Khudahs, the Lords of Bukhara. Qutaiba ibn Muslim finally seized the city, and the Arabs did not truly conquer it until after the Battle of Talas in 751.

The Samanids made it their capital in the 9th century and held it until 999, when the Karakhanids toppled them. The city was included in the Karakhanid state in 1005. It then belonged to the Khwarazm Shahs until Genghis Khan took it in 1220, and afterwards to the Chagatai Khanate and the Timurid Empire.

The Khanate of Bukhara took its name when the capital of the Shaybanid state was moved there, and it reached its greatest extent under Abdullah Khan II, who ruled from 1577 to 1598. Nadir Shah conquered it in 1740. After his death the khanate was controlled by the descendants of Khudayar Bi through the office of ataliq, and in 1785 Shah Murad formalised the family's dynastic rule, the Manghit dynasty, and the khanate became the Emirate of Bukhara. The emirate was a colonial acquisition of the Russian Empire.
sections.life:
Bukhara was multi-ethnic and multi-religious. When the Arabs arrived in 650 they found a decentralised collection of peoples, and before the Arab invasion the city sheltered followers of two religious movements persecuted within the Sasanian Empire, Manicheanism and Nestorian Christianity. Many coins with Christian symbols have been found in and around Bukhara, more than anywhere else in Central Asia. Narshakhi recorded that the people became Muslims but apostatised each time the Muslims withdrew, until Qutaiba established Islam there after much difficulty. For a century after the Battle of Talas Islam took root slowly. The Bukharan Jews, whose ancestors settled in the city during Roman times, mostly left between 1925 and 2000.

The city was a centre of learning. Under the Samanids New Persian flourished there, and a Samanid edict declared that in this region the language was Persian. Imam Bukhari, the compiler of hadiths, and Avicenna lived there. Omar Khayyam worked in Bukhara for a time at the invitation of the Karakhanid ruler Shams al-Mulk, and Baha-ud-Din Naqshband, a central figure of the Naqshbandi Sufi order, came from one of its neighbourhoods.

Water came from ponds, the hauzes, which also spread disease and were mostly filled in by the Soviets in the 1920s and 1930s. The Lab-i Hauz survived as the centrepiece of an ensemble of the 16th and 17th centuries. For several centuries Bukhara and Khiva were major centres of the slave trade.
sections.crises:
The Khwarazm Shahs, who held Bukhara, had killed the ambassador of the Mongols, and in 1220 Genghis Khan besieged the city for fifteen days. According to Juvaini, Genghis Khan contented himself with looting and slaughter once and did not go to the extreme of a general massacre, because the population readily submitted while the garrison in the citadel resisted. Most of the city burned. He spared most adults, killed 30,000 Qangli Turks on account of their loyalty to Sultan Muhammad, and conscripted all remaining able-bodied men.

The city recovered slowly. Ibn Battuta, passing through the region around 1333, found that the town had not recovered from being sacked, that its mosques, colleges and bazaars were in ruins, and that no one in it had religious learning or showed concern for acquiring it. By the 19th century it had become a peripheral city of the Persian and Islamic world. Charles Stoddart and Arthur Conolly, held there by the emir during the Great Game, were thrown into a vermin pit for months and then beheaded outside the citadel.

In 1920, during the Russian Civil War, Red Army troops under Mikhail Frunze attacked the city. On 31 August the emir, Mohammed Alim Khan, fled to Dushanbe, and on 2 September, after four days of fighting, the Ark was destroyed and the red flag was raised from the top of the Kalan Minaret. In 1922 most of Bukhara temporarily fell into the hands of the Basmachis during Enver Pasha's campaign.
sections.legacy:
Bukhara has about 140 architectural monuments, and its historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Ismail Samani mausoleum, built between 892 and 943, combines Zoroastrian and Islamic motifs, and the mausoleum of Muhammad Ali Jinnah in Karachi was modelled after it. It was said to have been buried in mud from flooding when the Mongols came, so that they spared it. The Karakhanid ruler Arslan Khan ordered the Kalan Minaret, which is 45.6 metres high and was designed by an architect named Bako. The Magok-i-Attari Mosque has a south facade of the 12th century, one of the oldest surviving structures in the city.

The Uzbek period added the Kalan Mosque, arguably completed in 1514 and able to hold twelve thousand people, the Mir-i Arab Madrasah of 1535 to 1536, and the Lab-i Hauz ensemble of 1568 to 1622. The Bolo Haouz Mosque was built in 1712. The emirs' Shirbudun Palace was begun about 1870.

The city entered literature as Albracca in Boiardo's epic Orlando Innamorato of 1483. Bukhara is today the capital of Bukhara Region, and one of the two major centres, with Samarkand, of Uzbekistan's Tajik minority. Its population was recorded as 279,200 in 2019.

summary: Bukhara, on the Zeravshan River in Uzbekistan, was officially founded in 500 BCE and became a Silk Road trade centre and, under the Samanids, an intellectual centre of the Islamic world. Genghis Khan took it in 1220, and the Emirate of Bukhara ended in 1920.
references: H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (The Royal Asiatic Society, 1923)
James Pickett, Polymaths of Islam: Power and Networks of Knowledge in Central Asia (Cornell University Press, 2020)
notes: SAMANID DATE: the city article says Bukhara served as the Samanid capital 'by 850'; the history article says 'in 892'. I left the year out and wrote 'the 9th century' in text and in the event. The Ismail Samani mausoleum's own dates (892-943) are as the city article gives them.

MONGOL SACK 1220: the city article says 'followed by its complete destruction'; the history article says 'levelled' in one place but quotes Juvaini that Genghis Khan did not go to a general massacre and that most of the city burned. Because the articles call it destroyed or levelled while Juvaini (quoted in the history article) says no general massacre and most of the city burned, I gave only Juvaini's account with attribution and left out the words destroyed and levelled. Please read this paragraph first.

ARAB CONQUEST: 650 (arrival) and the mosque of 94/712-3 are from the history article (Narshakhi). It also says the Arabs did not truly conquer Bukhara until after Talas (751). I give 712 as the date of the mosque, not of the conquest.

START: 'officially founded in 500 BCE' (history article); the Shahnameh account is given as legend. The city article gives no founding date. Archaeology dates the three settlements to c. 700 BCE; I kept 500 BCE as the start.
'The silk trade ... the rapid growth of the city which ended around 350 CE' is as written in the history article; the Hua tribes taking the city after the Kushan fall is also as written.

Slave trade: the article says Bukhara and Khiva were 'referred to as the slave capitals of the world'; I wrote only that they were major centres of the slave trade. The Samanid slave trade 'main income of the state' is as given.
Muslim mercenaries to China 1070 / 1080: the figures 5,300 and 10,000 are the article's; the Amir Sayyid 'So-fei-er' left out.

Left out: population claims about Tajik annexation movement, ethnic percentages (the article says the official figures are disputed), notable people after the 13th century, sister cities, climate figures beyond precipitation, transport, the 1995 Char Minar collapse, Fitzroy Maclean, Tughshada, An Lushan. Kalan Mosque is 'arguably completed in 1514' in the article.

The article says the Samani mausoleum was 'said to have already been buried in mud' at the Mongol invasion; hedged accordingly. Nadir Shah 1740 and the Shaybanid dates (1506-1598) vs Abdullah Khan II (1577-1598) as given in the history article.

The history article names the Bukhara oasis city's name derived questions; I left names out of the text for space. 'Bukhara was devastated ... recovered under the Timurids' (city article lead) is reflected only as 'afterwards to the Chagatai Khanate and the Timurid Empire'.
